title: Calories 101
summary: What calories actually are, why energy balance matters, and why the type of food you eat is just as important as the amount.

steps.heading: What is a calorie?
steps.body: A calorie is simply a unit of energy. In nutrition, when we say a food has 200 calories, we mean it contains enough chemical energy to raise the temperature of one kilogram of water by one degree Celsius. Your body uses this energy to fuel everything — from breathing and thinking to walking and digesting food itself.

steps.heading: Where do calories come from?
steps.body: Three macronutrients provide calories: carbohydrates and protein each provide about 4 calories per gram, while fat provides 9 calories per gram. Alcohol adds 7 calories per gram but has no nutritional value. Vitamins, minerals, water, and fibre provide no calories on their own, but fibre does affect how quickly you absorb the calories in a meal.

steps.heading: Energy balance: the core idea
steps.body: Your body is always comparing energy in versus energy out. When you consistently eat more calories than you burn, the surplus is stored — primarily as body fat. When you consume fewer than you burn, your body draws on stored energy. This relationship is real and well-established, though it is more complex than a simple calculator because your body adapts to changes over time.

steps.heading: Not all calories behave the same
steps.body: A 200-calorie serving of chicken and a 200-calorie serving of biscuits both register the same on a calorie counter, but your body processes them differently. Protein triggers stronger satiety hormones and requires more energy to digest. Ultra-processed foods are often engineered to be easy to overeat. The source of your calories genuinely affects hunger, energy levels, and long-term health — not just your waistline.

steps.heading: Calorie density matters too
steps.body: Calorie density is how many calories are packed into a given weight of food. Vegetables and fruits have very low calorie density — you can eat a large volume and still consume relatively few calories. Oils, cheese, and processed snacks are energy-dense, meaning a small amount contains a lot of calories. Eating more low-density foods is one of the most practical tools for managing hunger without strict portion control.

steps.heading: A practical way to think about it
steps.body: Rather than obsessing over exact numbers, think of calories as a rough guide. Most adults need somewhere between 1,600 and 2,500 calories per day, depending on their size, age, and activity level. Awareness — not restriction — is the goal here. Understanding roughly what you're consuming helps you make more intentional choices without making food feel like a maths exam.

takeaway: Calories measure energy in food. Balance matters, but so does food quality — what you eat affects hunger, digestion, and energy levels in ways that go beyond the number on the label.
